item.title: A Toll Booth on the World's Oil Highway: Inside the Iran–Oman Plan to Reopen Hormuz
item.body:
The proposal now circulating among Gulf capitals is deceptively simple. Tankers heading into the Persian Gulf would use one designated inbound lane, monitored on the Iranian side. Tankers heading out would use a separate lane on the Omani side. Ships would clear a joint notification system before entering, and they would pay what the framework reportedly calls a "service fee" — money described as covering escort, traffic management, spill response and environmental monitoring.

Regional officials cited in recent reporting say the arrangement is close to final. If it holds, it would end the most disruptive interruption to global energy shipping in decades. It would also hand Tehran something it did not have before the fighting began: a formal, revenue-generating role in managing traffic through the single most important chokepoint in the world economy.

That is the tension at the center of this story, and it is why the plan has run into a wall in Washington. President Donald Trump has said publicly that the United States will not accept Iran charging ships to pass. The framework's supporters say the fee is a technical cost-recovery measure. Its critics say a toll is a toll, and that once it exists, it never goes away.

**A note on sourcing:** the details below reflect what officials and analysts have described publicly. No final text has been released, and the terms could change or collapse entirely. Readers should treat specifics as provisional.

---

## Why this particular stretch of water matters so much

The Strait of Hormuz is roughly 21 nautical miles across at its narrowest point — about the distance from Manhattan to the middle of Long Island. The usable shipping channels are far narrower: two lanes of about two miles each, separated by a two-mile buffer, threading between Iranian waters to the north and Omani territory to the south.

Through that gap moves something on the order of a fifth of the world's traded oil, along with a comparable share of seaborne liquefied natural gas, most of it from Qatar. Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE, Kuwait and Iran itself all ship the bulk of their crude through it. There are pipeline workarounds — Saudi Arabia's East-West line to the Red Sea and the UAE's line to Fujairah — but together they can carry only a fraction of normal Hormuz volumes.

There is no substitute route. That single fact is what makes the strait valuable, and what makes any change to who manages it a matter of global consequence rather than regional housekeeping.

## How the two-lane system would work

Under the framework as described, the arrangement rests on three pillars.

**Split sovereignty over traffic.** Inbound vessels would transit a corridor supervised from the Iranian side; outbound vessels would use an Omani-supervised corridor. Both countries would contribute to a joint coordination cell handling vessel notifications, scheduling and incident response.

**A notification-and-clearance step.** Ships would file details in advance — flag, cargo, ownership, destination. Supporters present this as standard maritime traffic management, similar in spirit to systems used in other busy waterways. Skeptics note that a clearance step is also a screening step, and screening is leverage.

**The fee.** Vessels would pay a per-transit charge, framed as compensation for security escort, navigational services and environmental protection. Reported figures have varied widely and none should be treated as settled.

Oman's participation is the element that makes the package politically viable. Muscat has spent decades as the region's quiet intermediary — on good terms with Tehran, Washington, Riyadh and others simultaneously. Its presence lets shipowners and insurers describe the arrangement as multilateral rather than as an Iranian tollgate, and it gives Gulf states a counterpart they are willing to deal with.

## The money is smaller than it sounds — and bigger

Run the arithmetic and the direct cost looks modest. A very large crude carrier holds roughly two million barrels. A fee in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars spreads out to a few cents per barrel — noise against a crude price in the dollars-per-barrel swing range on any given week. Charterers absorb worse every month from bunker fuel moves.

But the fee is not really where the cost lives. The cost lives in insurance.

War-risk premiums for Gulf transits reprice constantly against perceived threat, and during acute periods they have jumped by multiples, sometimes adding far more per voyage than any proposed service fee. If the framework genuinely stabilizes transits — if underwriters believe escorted, deconflicted passage means fewer incidents — premiums fall, and shipowners could come out ahead even after paying. That is the commercial argument its backers make, and it is not a weak one.

The counterargument is about precedent rather than price. A fee that is small today is still a fee, and a mechanism that exists can be adjusted. Tie the rate to a vessel's flag, owner or destination, and a traffic-management system becomes an instrument of policy. Nothing in the reported framework suggests that is the intent. Nothing in it would obviously prevent it either.

## The legal argument nobody fully wins

International law treats natural straits differently from canals, and that distinction explains most of the dispute.

The Suez and Panama canals are engineered waterways, built and maintained by states that legitimately charge for their use. Hormuz is a natural channel. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, ships enjoy a right of transit passage through straits used for international navigation, and the convention bars states bordering a strait from levying charges on foreign vessels solely for passing through. Fees for specific services actually rendered — pilotage, salvage, traffic control — sit in a narrower and more defensible category.

The complication is that the parties do not stand on identical ground. Iran signed UNCLOS but never ratified it and has long maintained positions on transit rights that differ from the American reading. The United States never ratified the convention either, yet treats its navigation provisions as binding customary law and has enforced that view with naval presence for decades.

So both sides can cite the law and mean different things. There is also a partial precedent working in Tehran's favor: under the Montreux Convention, Turkey levies cost-recovery charges on ships transiting its straits for services such as lighthouses and health inspection. The amounts are small and the legal basis is specific, but the principle — a strait state charging for services — is established.

Expect the final text, if there is one, to be drafted with enormous care around a single word: whether the payment is for *passage* or for *services*.

## What each side gets

For Iran, the appeal is straightforward. A recognized administrative role converts pressure into position, generates revenue outside sanctioned oil channels, and creates a standing arrangement that would be politically awkward to unwind later.

For Gulf exporters, reopening restores the revenue their budgets depend on. Extended disruption is not a tolerable equilibrium for any producer in the region, including Iran.

For shipowners and cargo owners, predictability is the product. Commercial shipping does not need a favorable outcome so much as a legible one — a known rule, a known cost, a known route.

For Washington, the calculus is harder. Ending the disruption is a clear win. Accepting a permanent Iranian hand on the throttle of global energy trade is a clear loss. The administration's position appears to be that it can have the first without the second, which is why the fee — the smallest number in the package — has become the largest obstacle.

## What to watch

- **The wording.** "Service charge" versus "transit fee" is not semantics. It determines whether the arrangement can be described as consistent with existing law.
- **Who collects.** A jointly administered fund with published accounts reads very differently from direct payment to a national authority.
- **Whether it is flag-blind.** A uniform charge applied to all vessels is a traffic system. A differentiated one is leverage.
- **Duration and review.** A defined sunset with renewal conditions is a temporary fix. An open-ended arrangement is a new permanent feature of the map.
- **Insurance rates.** The most honest indicator of whether markets believe any of this will be what underwriters do with war-risk premiums, not what officials say at podiums.

## The bottom line

The choice on the table is between two imperfect outcomes: a closed or unreliable strait that damages nearly everyone, or an open strait on terms that leave Tehran with more standing than it held before. Neither is anyone's preferred result, and the negotiation is essentially about which imperfection is easier to live with.

The plan's real test is not whether it reopens the waterway. It is whether the mechanism that reopens it can be retired later — or whether the toll booth, once built, simply becomes part of the road.

---

*This article is an analytical explainer based on publicly reported information available at the time of writing. Terms described here are unconfirmed and subject to change. It is not investment, legal, or operational advice.*
